tasks.short: Find late and early refills, look for usage trends, review flagged patients, phone prescribers and talk with patients.

steps.what: Pharmacist runs queries in the pharmacy system for late and early refills
Pharmacist exports dispensing data to a spreadsheet to analyze prescribing trends
Pharmacist reviews flagged patients and decides what to do
Pharmacist phones prescribers about excessive usage or harmful interactions
Pharmacist talks with patients about compliance at the counter

tasks.design: Nightly rules in the pharmacy system ({OTHER}) compute days covered per chronic medicine, flag late and early refills and cumulative opioid doses above thresholds set by the pharmacist, and a dashboard shows usage trends per medicine and prescriber. The pharmacist reviews the flags and decides; calls to prescribers and talks with patients stay with the pharmacist. Interaction checks at dispensing continue as now.
tasks.previous_blocker: Trends needed ad-hoc queries and spreadsheet exports.
tasks.enabler_now: Dispensing data are complete and structured; adherence and dose rules are plain code.
tasks.still_hard: A late refill can have good reasons; flags are a start, not a finding.
tasks.human_edge: Hearing why a patient stopped taking a medicine.
tasks.altitude: The pharmacist reviews flags instead of building queries.

evidence.claim: The G-Standaard checks interactions, contraindications, doses and duplicates; KNMP sets the content.
Solely automated care decisions need a legal basis under GDPR article 22(2); flags go to the pharmacist.

assumptions: Boundary: from dispensing data to action with prescriber or patient; changes in therapy are outside.
Input contract: dispensing history recorded by the pharmacy system at each dispensing; thresholds set by the pharmacist; fallback is ad-hoc queries.
Calls and patient talks do not change.
Prescriber time is outside the pharmacist's savings.
unknowns: Flags per week at the chosen thresholds.
research_questions: Does adherence for flagged patients improve?

incremental.description: Pharmacist tunes flag thresholds each quarter.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Pharmacies with existing adherence reports save less.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Update patient profiles from hospital letters, keep the controlled drugs register, count and reconcile stock, and update inventory after deliveries.

steps.what: Pharmacist updates patient profiles with allergies and contraindications from hospital letters
Pharmacist writes receipts and dispensing of narcotics in the controlled drugs register
inputs: controlled drug packs received and dispensed

steps.what: Pharmacist counts controlled drug stock each week
Pharmacist investigates differences between count and register
Pharmacist checks deliveries against the wholesaler's delivery note and updates inventories

tasks.design: Hospital medication overviews arrive by structured exchange into the pharmacy system ({OTHER}), which proposes profile changes for the pharmacist to confirm. The pharmacist scans each controlled drug pack at receipt and dispensing and the system writes the register line. The wholesaler's electronic delivery note is loaded as expected stock; the pharmacist checks the received goods against it, records shortages and damage, and the inventory is updated from the confirmed receipt. Weekly counts and investigating differences stay with the pharmacist.
tasks.previous_blocker: Letters, registers and deliveries were entered by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Pharmacy systems take structured medication overviews, scans and electronic delivery notes.
tasks.still_hard: Count differences need investigation; structured exchange does not reach every hospital.
tasks.human_edge: Spotting a pattern in register differences that points to misuse.

reach.learn: Whether electronic delivery notes remove manual entry.

evidence.claim: Pharmacy systems record controlled-drug movements from scans and inventory from electronic delivery notes.
The patient dossier is kept twenty years after the last change.
Pharmacies must keep a register of controlled drugs under the Opium Act.

assumptions: Boundary: from incoming information to updated records; audits by the inspectorate are outside.

Input contract: medication overviews sent by hospital pharmacies; electronic delivery notes sent by the wholesaler give dispatched lines only; received quantities come from the pharmacist's goods-in check; fallback is manual entry.
Register lines are written from the pharmacist's own scans of the packs actually received and dispensed.
Counting and investigating do not change.
Assistant time is outside the pharmacist's savings.
unknowns: Share of hospitals sending structured overviews.

already_counted.description: Pharmacist scans controlled drug packs at receipt and dispensing.
Pharmacist checks received goods against the delivery note and records differences.

incremental.description: Pharmacist checks scan errors in the register.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a pharmacy whose system already loads delivery notes, so only the register and profiles change; high: a pharmacy writing the register by hand and receiving structured hospital overviews.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Check certificates of analysis against specifications, test raw material identity, inspect finished preparations, record results and release or reject the batch.

steps.what: Pharmacist checks each supplier certificate of analysis against the pharmacopoeia limits

loop.input: The supplier's certificate of analysis for a raw material batch, as a PDF.
loop.output: The test names, results and units in a check sheet.
loop.check: Code compares each extracted result with the specification limits kept by the pharmacy and flags any value out of range or missing; the pharmacist verifies every extracted value against the certificate.
loop.stop: One extraction per certificate; unreadable certificates go to manual checking.
loop.why_not_simpler: Certificates come in many supplier layouts; a fixed template cannot read them.

steps.what: Pharmacist performs identity tests on raw materials
Pharmacist inspects finished preparations for appearance, weight and strength
Pharmacist writes test results in the batch record by hand
Pharmacist releases or rejects the batch

tasks.design: A bounded step reads each supplier certificate into a check sheet, and code compares the values with the pharmacy's specification limits; the pharmacist verifies the values. Balances and the spectrometer write their results into the electronic batch record ({OTHER}) instead of hand copying. Identity tests, inspection and release stay with the pharmacist.
tasks.previous_blocker: Certificates were checked line by line and results copied by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Lab instruments export results, and language models can read varied PDF layouts.
tasks.still_hard: A misread value could pass a bad batch; the pharmacist must verify every value.
tasks.human_edge: Noticing a powder that looks slightly wrong despite a clean certificate.
tasks.altitude: The pharmacist verifies extracted values instead of reading every certificate line.

evidence.claim: Lab balances and spectrometers can export results to batch records.
Providers are responsible for careful use of generative AI: assess risks, test and monitor.

assumptions: Boundary: from incoming certificates to the batch decision; supplier qualification is outside.
Input contract: certificates sent by suppliers with each batch; specification limits kept by the pharmacist from the pharmacopoeia; fallback is manual checking.
Testing, inspecting and release do not change.
research_questions: How often does extraction misread a value?

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Pharmacies that rarely compound save little.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Write and update procedures, track review dates, train staff, collect read-and-sign records, audit on the floor and arrange disposal.

steps.what: Pharmacist writes and updates procedures for mixing, packaging and labeling
Pharmacist tracks procedure review dates in a spreadsheet
Pharmacist trains assistants on new procedures
Pharmacist collects staff signatures on paper for read procedures
Pharmacist audits work on the floor against the procedures
Pharmacist arranges proper disposal of expired medicines and records it on a form

tasks.design: Procedures live in a document control space ({DOCS}) with versions and review dates that send reminders, and staff confirm each new version with read-and-sign in the same place, so no paper signatures are chased. Disposal is recorded in a short form there. Writing procedures, training, floor audits and arranging disposal stay with the pharmacist.
tasks.previous_blocker: Review dates were in a spreadsheet and signatures on paper.
tasks.enabler_now: Document control tools hold versions, review dates and read-and-sign records.
tasks.still_hard: Signing is not understanding; floor audits stay needed.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing on the floor that a procedure does not work in practice.

evidence.claim: Document control tools hold procedure versions, review dates and read-and-sign records.
Read-and-sign logs show what each staff member has read; using them to judge staff needs works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from requirements to audited practice and disposal; inspections are outside.
Input contract: legal requirements from the professional standards kept by the pharmacist; staff list from HR; fallback is paper.
Writing, training and audits do not change.
Staff reading time is outside the pharmacist's savings.
research_questions: Are procedures reviewed on time more often?

incremental.description: Pharmacist moves procedures into the document space once.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Most of this task is writing, training and audits.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The pharmacist keeps clinical judgement, testing and release; queries, registers, copying and paper signatures go.
role.ambitious_version: A pharmacist who spends the saved time on medication reviews with patients.
